variants.name: Patchwork Pocha
variants.prompt:
Use case: stylized-concept.
Asset type: original environment concept art for the Three.js game Seoul Snack Attack. This is a visual-direction proposal for a buildable 3D game environment.
Primary request: a quirky, off-beat FOUR-storey Seoul corner building with a welcoming late-night Korean snack shop at street level, realistic depth and tangible stylized PBR materials, suitable for a lively delivery-driving game.
Scene and program shared across the three design directions: a roughly 12-metre by 10-metre corner footprint; exactly ONE ground floor plus THREE upper storeys. Shop has a recessed corner entrance, genuinely transparent deep shop windows, visible stainless cooking counter, a few stools, shelves and warm interior lights. The upper three floors are small apartments/workshops. Separate upper-floor entrance. One small rooftop utility element, not an extra fifth storey. Sidewalk on both street-facing sides, a real curb, drainage grate, tactile pavers, and a modest wet asphalt street corner. Recognizably Seoul through architecture, services and Hangul signage. Two muted neighboring buildings recede in the background; the single hero building remains dominant.
Composition: landscape 3:2 image; one uninterrupted main view, no collage. Consistent three-quarter corner view from across the intersection, looking slightly down from approximately 16 m camera height at a target 7 m high, 45 mm lens. Show the full building, the rooftop silhouette and both street-facing facades, with breathing room on every side, pavement and some road foreground. Entire building occupies about 70 percent of image height. No cropped roof or cut-off base.
Lighting: bright late blue-hour twilight immediately after rain; a softly lavender sky, warm shop light spilling onto the sidewalk, readable facade exposure and neutral enough fill to judge the actual paint. Local highlights on wet patches, gentle restrained bloom. Rich shadows retain architectural detail.
Craft: finished, high-quality stylized 3D environment concept. Designed shapes with slight exaggeration and tactile, believable surfaces: real window reveals and frame thickness, modeled tile edges, bevels, modest roughness variation, localized age and rain streaks at joints. Each material responds differently to light. Detail is composed into clear shapes and clusters; strong readable silhouette and lovely small discoveries.
Text, exactly: main shop fascia “밤참 분식”; one small menu reads “떡볶이”. Use clear legible Hangul only for these two signs, and pictograms for other small labels. No extra English text, branding, title, watermark or interface overlay.
Constraints: no people, no vehicles; the architecture is the subject. No copied commercial characters or brands. Keep the structural floors and shop entrance usable and plausible. No disconnected floating elements, impossible stairs, razor-sharp primitive boxes, wallpaper windows, unreadable black storefront, excessive neon, uniform grunge/noise, photorealistic bland office architecture, or toy-plastic materials on every surface. The rooftop feature must attach credibly to the building.

Direction A — PATCHWORK POCHA:
Warm, scrappy, inhabited and affectionately eccentric. The main structure is rich old russet brick with weathered mortar, patched creamy plaster and several dusty jade-painted repairs. A facade assembled across decades: different but carefully aligned window types, a slim enclosed jade balcony on the second floor, a tiny projecting bay on the third, and a fourth-storey brick parapet whose crown steps gently. Modest, physically supported asymmetry, with large readable shapes.
At ground level: an aged oxblood and cream striped fabric awning, warm ivory tiled entrance surround with jade base tiles, hand-painted enamel main sign and a comically oversized sculpted tteokbokki rice-cake-on-a-fork projecting sign mounted at the corner. The rice cake is a simple original rounded expressive food mascot, with tiny sleepy eyes; not an animal. Roof has one little corrugated utility shed and an old green water tank, with grouped ceramic kimchi pots and a few plants. Copper-brown drainpipes, sensible AC brackets, repaired conduit, a short line of small lanterns under the awning. A little eccentricity in every renovation, no structural collapse. Let the comedy come from handmade proportions and affectionate accumulated repairs. Finish should feel warm and tactile, sophisticated enough for a game hero asset.

Direction B — SNACKWAVE:
Bold, cheeky retro design with grounded materials. A Korean neighborhood commercial building reimagined with generously rounded CORNERS, stepped asymmetrical facade sections and thick rounded window frames. Exactly four distinct storeys. Main colors: toasted cream plaster, avocado/jade glazed tile panels, muted strawberry-lilac accent sections and a controlled persimmon-orange storefront trim. Warm grey structural sides. Avoid a rainbow: cream and jade are dominant, lilac and orange appear in deliberate local accents.
Ground-floor frontage wraps the corner in glazed jade ceramic tiles, with rounded cream portal frames, a deep orange-edged canopy, warm translucent ribbed glass, a cozy snack counter and an oversized dimensional main sign mounted cleanly above the canopy. The memorable hero detail is an ORIGINAL lilac hippo mascot corner sign: a squat round hippo head with tiny round ears, bulging friendly eyes and a broad goofy open mouth holding a small steaming snack bowl. The hippo is a sculpted enamel sign supported on a visible metal bracket at the building's second-storey corner, not a huge animal sitting on the entire roof. Its silhouette reads from a moving vehicle.
Upper windows form a playful, deliberately offset rhythm with rounded rectangular openings and real recesses. One slim balcony has bent tubular railings. Rooftop is a sculptural stepped parapet with a compact jade utility housing, one short rounded vent, a small TV aerial, no extra storey. A circular orange clock sign and a few graphic food pictograms add restrained retro appliance/cassette-player character. Tile grout, enamel edge chips, satin powder-coated railings, rough plaster and slight fabric creasing should all be visible. This is confident, eccentric architecture, not a generic cute miniature.

Direction C — MIDNIGHT SNACK LAB:
An eccentric improvised food workshop that became a neighborhood institution. A four-storey early-modern Seoul concrete building with a slightly stepped outline, generous deep square windows, exposed structural lintels, hand-repaired ceramic tile cladding and believable industrial services. A warm off-white concrete shell, deep petrol-teal square tiles on the lower two floors, locally faded butter-yellow painted frames, small chili-orange details and cool grey metal. More wiry and mechanical than the other designs, but inviting and funny.
Ground-floor shop is tucked behind thick tiled piers and a patched curved sheet-metal canopy with warm bulbs. Its recessed corner entrance and windows reveal a busy little cooking counter with visible stainless-steel pots, shelves and soft steam in the interior. Main sign is warm-backlit enamel with exactly the specified Hangul. A few robust exterior service pipes travel visibly from the shop toward the roof in tidy but peculiar bends; all pipes have supports, connections and plausible destinations. No random pipe spaghetti.
The unforgettable rooftop object is a FUNCTIONAL-LOOKING VENTILATOR designed like a giant battered yellow enamel cooking pot with a tilted lid and small side handles; a narrow puff of steam escapes from its chimney. It is bolted to a compact metal service platform behind the parapet and integrated with the ductwork. Pot width is roughly 3 m against the 12 m facade, not a building-sized hat. A few air conditioning units sit on an organized side rack. One little orange service ladder rises to the roof with a proper landing; one upper bay has a cozy amber-lit workshop behind frosted glass.
The humor is the exaggerated culinary machinery and accumulated practical inventions. Clear strong architectural forms, rich ceramic and metal texture, slight hand-built wonkiness, no dystopian grime, no cyberpunk billboard overload. It should feel like a beloved oddball local restaurant with a secret obsession with making the perfect midnight snack.
